chunks: From him, from Fadalah ibn Ayyub, from Rifa'ah ibn Musa, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the dog that kills [game], and he said, 'Eat it.' I said, 'It ate from it [the prey],' and he said, 'If it ate from it and did not hold back [the saliva/impurity] upon you, it only held back upon itself.' These two reports are understood to be [applicable] when the dog is accustomed to eating the prey, because if it is so, it is not permissible to eat from what it ate from it. As for if that is unusual for it, then there is no harm with it, according to what we have previously stated. And it is possible that they came out as a form of precautionary dissimulation (taqiyyah), because among the general public is one who says it is not permissible to eat the prey if it ate from it, because it would have held back upon itself and not held back upon you. And Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) clarified the invalidity of that in the report narrated from him by Hakim ibn Hukaym, which we have previously presented. And that which also indicates the permissibility of that, added to what we have presented, is what he narrated:
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on eating game killed by a dog if the dog eats from the prey?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies the permissibility of consuming game killed by a hunting dog, distinguishing between habitual and occasional eating to resolve apparent contradictions in juristic opinions. The text highlights the scholarly debate on whether the ruling reflects *taqiyyah* to accommodate the general public's view that the prey becomes impure if the dog consumes part of it. This analysis underscores the nuanced approach of Shia jurisprudence in reconciling textual evidence with practical social considerations.
